Akron by the numbers

Who bills property tax for a house in Akron, Ohio?

Akron sits in Summit County, and the county bills the tax through its Fiscal Office. One elected fiscal officer runs three divisions there: the Auditor values property, the Treasurer collects and chases late payments, and the Recorder files deeds.

The office announced a temporary move out of the Ohio Building at 175 S. Main St. while that building is renovated, with the stay described as lasting until late 2026. Check the fiscal office site for the counter address before any in-person trip.

When is the second-half Akron property tax due?

Summit County collects real estate tax in two halves, with the second half due in July. For the second half of 2025, bills went out starting June 24, 2026, later than in earlier years, and the closing date for payment was Friday, July 31, 2026. The fiscal office tied the delay to Ohio House Bill 186, which created an Inflation Cap Credit for taxpayers in certain school districts that sit on the 20-mill floor and for joint vocational districts on the 2-mill floor, and which forced a one-time recalculation of rates.

The same notice says a payment mailed in must carry a U.S. postmark on or before the due date to avoid the statutory 10 percent late penalty, and a private postage meter does not count. Ohio law puts the duty on the owner to get and pay the bill, so call 330-643-2588 for a copy if one does not arrive.

What ways can you pay an Akron tax bill?

The Summit County notice lists four routes:

  • In person at the Treasurer Division counter.
  • By mail, with the postmark rule above.
  • Online or by phone through ACI Payments, with a service fee for cards and a $1 fee for e-checks. Have the parcel number ready.
  • At participating banks in the Regional Tax Collection System. The branch must be in Summit County, and not every bank takes cash.

Owners who cannot pay in full can use the Tax Installment Program if all taxes and assessments are current and the parcel is owner-occupied; the number to enroll is (330) 643-2869. Separately, the Real Estate Discount program lets a taxpayer pay toward a half in monthly coupons and earn a credit based on county investment yield. Enrollment runs July 1 to October 31 for the first half and January 1 to March 31 for the second half, and taxes must be current. Military reservists on active duty can defer taxes; the number for that application is (330) 643-2641.

What if the Akron tax is already delinquent?

Summit County's Delinquent Tax Payment Plan, started in 1987, lets an owner who missed a first or second half payment set up monthly installments. Once the plan begins, the delinquent balance is frozen in a special account with no further interest, and the extra interest is abated when the plan is completed. The owner must still pay current taxes as they come due. The Delinquent Tax Department is at 330-643-2600.

The county's Tax Certificate Liens page warns that to avoid a sale of a tax certificate lien on a parcel, the taxes must be paid in full or a payment plan arranged, and that fees and costs of a certificate sale may fall on the owner. Ask the Treasurer Division for a payoff figure before the closing date so the title company can include it.

How do you contest an Akron home value?

The Summit County Board of Revision hears complaints about value. Forms are accepted from January 1 to March 31, by U.S. Mail postmarked by the deadline, in person, or online through the county's Smartfile system. Questions go to bor@summitoh.net or 330-926-2559.

  • The board's members are the fiscal officer, the county executive and the clerk of courts, or their representatives.
  • Filing starts a legal proceeding, and the owner carries the burden of proof with supporting documents.
  • The board does not hear complaints about the tax itself, only the valuation.

The official page adds that Ohio law calls for a reappraisal every six years with an update in the third year. New construction is added at cost, though routine upkeep such as a new roof does not raise the appraisal while structural work on wiring, plumbing, framing or foundation may.

Which tax breaks can an Akron homeowner use?

The fiscal office describes the Homestead Exemption as removing the first $29,000 of appraised value from taxation for a single-family home, with an average saving of $535 a year. Eligible veterans with a 100 percent service-connected disability rating get an extra exemption on the first $58,000. Applicants over 65 or permanently and totally disabled must stay under a household income cap, listed as $40,000 for 2025 applications and $41,000 for 2026, and the information line is (330) 643-2661.

The owner-occupancy credit lowers the tax charged by qualified levies on a principal residence. The office asks for applications by December 31 of the year you qualify, rental properties are ineligible, and the reduction stays only until the property transfers or stops being the owner's residence. Because of that, ask the fiscal office what credits your parcel currently has before you list it.

What fees apply when an Akron house changes hands?

The county's Property Transfer Department approves the legal description and conveyance, and it accepts DTE Form 100, the statement of value and receipt, plus DTE Form 100 (EX) for exempt transfers. The page asks for properly prepared forms by 3:30 p.m. for same-day transfer of title, citing ORC 319.202 and 319.54(G)(3).

Summit County Fiscal Office fees for a property transfer, as printed on its fee page
ItemFee printed by the office
Conveyance fee$4.00 per $1000, rounded up to the next $100 of the sale price
Lot fee50 cents per lot in the legal description, exempt or not
Basic recording$34.00 for 2 pages, $8.00 each added page
Non-compliant document$20.00 per document
Cross reference$4.00 each

Whether the seller or the buyer pays each item is a matter for the purchase contract, so ask the title company how it will split them on the settlement statement.

What should an owner know about Akron itself?

Akron lies about 39 miles south of Lake Erie on the Glaciated Allegheny Plateau, bordered by Cuyahoga Falls on the north and Barberton to the southwest. The Ohio and Erie Canal runs through the city and splits east from west. The town was laid out in December 1825 at the summit of that canal, the name coming from the Greek word for summit, and it became the Summit County seat in 1841 and a city in 1865. Tire makers made it the Rubber Capital of the World, and Goodyear Heights and Firestone Park were built as company neighborhoods for rubber workers. Kenmore was annexed in 1928.

The economy leans on health care, higher education and polymers. Top employers listed in the city's 2020 financial report include Summa Health System, the University of Akron, Akron Children's Hospital, FirstEnergy, Akron General and Akron Public Schools. Public school students attend the Akron City School District, which is partway through a 15-year, $800 million rebuilding program.

  • Population: 189,691 in July 2025, down 0.4 percent from the April 2020 base.
  • Owner-occupied rate: 50.7 percent, against 67.5 percent for Summit County.
  • Median owner-occupied value: $122,000, compared with $208,700 countywide.
  • Median household income: $48,076; median gross rent: $955.
  • Land area: 61.93 square miles, about 3,075 residents per square mile in 2020.

The figures come from Census QuickFacts. With about half of Akron's homes rented, a seller with a tenant in place should settle the lease question before listing.

More questions about Akron, OH Property Tax Guide

Who do I pay Akron property tax to?

You pay the Summit County Fiscal Office, Treasurer Division. The City of Akron sits inside Summit County, and the county bills and collects the tax.

What was the due date for second-half 2025 Akron property tax?

It was Friday, July 31, 2026, with bills mailed beginning June 24, 2026. Mailed payments had to carry a U.S. postmark by that date to avoid the 10 percent penalty.

When can I file a Board of Revision complaint in Akron?

Forms are accepted from January 1 through March 31, by mail with a postmark by the deadline, in person, or online through Smartfile. Call 330-926-2559 with questions.

What is the conveyance fee when I sell in Akron?

The Fiscal Office prints $4.00 per $1000, rounded up to the next $100 of the sale price, plus a 50 cent lot fee for each lot in the legal description.

What can I do about delinquent property tax in Akron?

Call the Delinquent Tax Department at 330-643-2600 about the Delinquent Tax Payment Plan. It freezes the balance with no further interest while you pay it in monthly installments and keep current taxes paid.

Cash Home Buyers in Ohio
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Cincinnati, OH Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is

Owe Cincinnati Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who bills what in Cincinnati

  • Hamilton County Auditor handles assessment.

Due dates

Real estate taxes are paid twice a year in February and July. For 2026 the second half was moved: bills mailed July 2, due July 24, 2026 (Treasurer press release).. See the official page.

Challenging your assessment

Complete DTE 1 (or DTE 1M for manufactured homes) and submit between Jan 1 and Mar 31, 2026 (postmarked no later than Mar 31).. See the official page.

Local notes

  • Late penalty per Treasurer page: 5% first 10 days after due date, then 10%.
Behind on Cincinnati property tax?
We buy Cincinnati houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.
Get My Cash Offer →

Cincinnati by the numbers

Which offices tax a Cincinnati house?

A Cincinnati homeowner never pays the city for property tax. The bill comes from Hamilton County, where the auditor sets each parcel's market value and the treasurer does the billing and banking. Treasurer staff work from Room 402 of the building at 138 East Court Street and answer 513-946-4800 on weekdays during daytime hours, 8 to 4.

Disagreements over value are heard by a three-member Board of Revision. According to the treasurer's real estate page, its seats go to the auditor, the treasurer and the commissioners' president. The city levies tax and receives its share of the proceeds, yet it does not value or bill the house.

When were the 2026 Cincinnati property tax bills due?

The treasurer's home page shows the 2026 calendar: first-half bills out on January 16 with payment due February 10, then second-half bills out July 2 with payment due July 24. The second pair was a late change. A June 22, 2026 press release said state legislation requiring an Inflation Cap Credit forced a recalculation of the second-half bills, which pushed the schedule back.

  • Bills come twice a year, and each prints its own deadline.
  • Ten days of grace carry a 5 percent penalty, and anything later carries 10 percent.
  • Owners who want a penalty reviewed can download a Penalty Remit Application from the treasurer's site.
  • Paying early earns no discount. A prepayment program called TOP lets owners pay ahead in installments.

Future years may land on different dates, so check the bill and the treasurer's site each cycle.

What are the ways to pay a Cincinnati tax bill?

The office accepts payment four ways, according to its payment page.

  • Online with Point & Pay. The vendor, not the county, charges $1.00 for an eCheck or 2.35 percent on a credit card.
  • By telephone to the same vendor, 1-877-764-3524.
  • By mail: a personal check, cashier's check or money order made out to Hamilton County Treasurer, with the stub or parcel number on the memo line.
  • At the Room 402 counter, which is also the only place that takes cash.

Mail is on time when postmarked by the due date. The payment page cautions that the Postal Service postmark now reflects the day a machine sorts the envelope, which may be after you dropped it off. Close to a deadline, hand the envelope to a clerk and ask for a manual stamp.

How is a Cincinnati tax bill built from levies?

The treasurer's glossary walks through the pieces. Assessed value is 35 percent of market value, and every rate is quoted in mills, with a mill equal to $1 per $1,000 of assessed value. A reduction factor keeps each voted levy near the revenue voters approved, which blunts the effect of rising values. After that come state credits: the non-business credit for residential property, the owner occupancy credit and the homestead credit.

The same page lists the countywide levies that show on a Cincinnati bill. The bill adds separate school district, township and city or village lines. One quirk from the page: Great Oaks career campus levies apply in every Hamilton County school district except Cincinnati and Northwest.

Selected Hamilton County levies as printed on the Hamilton County Treasurer's real estate page
LevyMillsTerm noted
County general fund2.26Continuing
Public library2.501.00 expires tax year 2027, 1.50 expires 2033
Developmental disabilities4.13Expires tax year 2028
Park district1.980.03 continuing, 0.95 expires 2030
Crime information center0.54Continuing
Zoological park0.46Expires tax year 2027

A Rate of Taxation download on the same page shows the rate for your own taxing district.

How do you challenge a Cincinnati property value?

Owners who think the auditor's market value is too high file with the Board of Revision from January 1 to March 31. The treasurer's page repeats that window and directs filers to the board's website for forms, and its FAQ gives 513-946-4035 as the board's phone. Section 5715.19 backs the deadline: March 31 of the year after the tax year, or the end of first-half collection if later. A postmark by that day counts for mailed filings.

Only the market value can be contested. The treasurer's FAQ explains that a bill reflects local levies and market value together, and the levies are beyond a complaint's reach. Pending a decision, an owner may pay tax calculated on the lower value the complaint claims.

What can a Cincinnati owner do about delinquent taxes?

The delinquent taxes page describes what follows a missed payment. Penalties and interest begin immediately. A taxpayer can phone 513-946-4800 and request a delinquent contract, which spreads past-due amounts into scheduled payments while current bills are paid on time. Staying in good standing on the contract shields the house from further penalties, interest, foreclosure and a lien sale.

  • Balances left after the second-half collection are certified delinquent that November. They can enter a lien sale the following October, typically near the middle of the month.
  • Eligible liens go to financial institutions in one negotiated block, not one at a time to individuals, and extra fees attach once a lien is sold.
  • A tax foreclosure is a lawsuit brought by the county prosecutor. Owners typically get 28 days to respond to the summons, and a judgment leads to an online sheriff's sale.

Cincinnati owners had one extra option in 2025. A county news release of August 18, 2025 announced a single-run, city-funded program, carried out with the Landbank and a nonprofit counseling group, to buy and retire delinquent liens for about 250 homeowners before the 2025 bills came due in 2026. The qualifying house was an owner-occupied single or two-family home worth no more than $100,000, with delinquent taxes of $10,000 or less in July 2025. Letters went to qualifying owners.

Which credits can lower a Cincinnati tax bill?

Ohio's homestead exemption reaches Cincinnati owners through the county auditor. The state tax department puts the 2026 credit at the tax on $29,700 of value for qualifying seniors and disabled owners whose income is within $41,000, and at $59,400 for disabled veterans, who face no income test.

Another credit needs no application: the treasurer's FAQ says the stadium sales tax credit comes automatically to owners already getting the 2.5 percent rollback on an owner-occupied home. File the homestead paperwork by December 31 of the year you want it, as the state FAQ explains.

What is Cincinnati like for a house seller?

Downtown Cincinnati occupies flat ground by the Ohio River, facing the mouth of Kentucky's Licking River, and the rest of the city climbs over hills and ridges. Fifty-two neighborhoods make up the city. Over-the-Rhine, built largely by German immigrants between 1865 and the 1880s, is among the largest intact urban historic districts in the country, and Westwood has the most residents. Norwood, Elmwood Place and St. Bernard are enclaves inside the city limits and have their own governments, so check which jurisdiction a street belongs to. Since 1922 the official Ohio flood stage at Cincinnati has been 52 feet, and the river's record crest came in January 1937.

  • Population estimate for July 2025: 314,367, which is 1.5 percent more than in April 2020.
  • Owners hold 39.8 percent of homes (2020 to 2024).
  • Typical value of an owner's home: $230,900.
  • Household income at the midpoint: $52,909, and 25.5 percent of people in poverty.
  • Gross rent at the midpoint: $1,001, among 144,297 households.

The figures above are from Census QuickFacts. Because owners hold fewer than four in ten homes, a seller may be a landlord or an heir, who should check the tax status of each parcel.

How does a tax bill affect a fast sale in Cincinnati?

An unpaid half-year stays on the parcel, and the buyer's title search will turn it up. Get a payoff figure from the treasurer that covers prior years, then pass it to whoever runs the closing. If a lien was already sold, the treasurer's office will name the purchaser, and the payoff then includes that holder's added fees.

An owner who is behind but wants to keep the house can sign a delinquent contract before the lien sale, which keeps the parcel out of it provided current taxes are paid.

More questions about Cincinnati, OH Property Tax Guide

What number reaches the office that sends Cincinnati tax bills?

Dial 513-946-4800 for the Hamilton County Treasurer, open weekdays. Value questions go to the Board of Revision at 513-946-4035, a number the treasurer's FAQ provides.

Which day was the 2026 second-half Cincinnati deadline?

July 24, 2026. Bills were mailed July 2. The date was moved from the usual schedule because state law required an Inflation Cap Credit to be built into the second-half bills.

What penalty applies to a late Cincinnati property tax payment?

Five percent during the first ten days after the due date, then 10 percent, as the treasurer's real estate page states. A Penalty Remit Application is available on the site.

What is the filing window for a Cincinnati value complaint?

January 1 through March 31. The complaint goes to the Hamilton County Board of Revision, and mail dated by March 31 counts.

Can unpaid taxes cost me my Cincinnati house?

Only through foreclosure. A lien sale moves the lien, not the house, and the holder may start foreclosure after a year. A delinquent contract signed before the sale, with current taxes paid, keeps the parcel off the list.

Cash Home Buyers in Ohio
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Cleveland, OH Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Cleveland, OH Property Tax Guide sale

Owe Cleveland Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who bills what in Cleveland

  • Cuyahoga County Fiscal Officer - Real Property Department handles assessment.

Due dates

Tax Collection Calendar: first half 2025 (pay 2026) real estate taxes due Feb 19; second half due Aug 13 (2026).. See the official page.

Challenging your assessment

Board of Revision valuation complaint may be filed Jan 1 through Mar 31 each year (next business day if Mar 31 is a weekend); e-file preferred, also mail/email/fax; mailed complaints need USPS postmark of Mar 31 or earlier.. See the official page.

Local notes

Behind on Cleveland property tax?
We buy Cleveland houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.
Get My Cash Offer →

Cleveland by the numbers

Which county offices value and bill a Cleveland house?

County government, not city hall, runs real estate tax on a Cleveland house. Cuyahoga County's Fiscal Officer appraises each parcel, and the county Treasurer bills and collects.

Both offices sit in the Cuyahoga County Administrative Building at 2079 East 9th Street, Cleveland, Ohio 44115: the appraisal department on the third floor, the cashier on the first, and Transfer and Recording on the fourth. The Treasurer's taxpayer line is 216-443-7400, option 1. MyPlace, the county's online property search, lets you pull up a parcel and view its taxes.

Four things build a bill: the millage in your taxing district, any special assessments, the property's value, and reduction credits such as owner occupancy and homestead. Only the value is open to a Board of Revision complaint.

What should a Cleveland seller know about the city itself?

Cleveland lies along Lake Erie's southern shore, on a run of bluffs broken by the Cuyahoga River, Big Creek and Euclid Creek. The city covers about 82 square miles including water and was founded in 1796 near the river mouth. It is the second most populous city in Ohio.

The City Planning Commission recognizes 34 neighborhoods, and residents sort themselves by the river into an East Side and a West Side. Ohio City, Tremont, Detroit-Shoreway and Edgewater on the west, and Collinwood, Hough, Fairfax and Little Italy on the east, have drawn new residents back in recent years. Inner suburbs such as Lakewood, Shaker Heights, Cleveland Heights and Parma share its borders.

The Treasurer publishes residential and commercial rates for each community in the county, so check the taxing district printed on the bill before comparing a Cleveland house with one in a neighboring suburb.

What are the Cleveland tax dates for 2026, and what happens after them?

The Treasurer's 2026 calendar lists February 19 as the first-half due date and August 13 as the second-half due date. Both dates have passed. Ten percent penalties were assessed on March 2 and August 23, and interest of 9% on prior-year delinquent real estate tax attached September 1, with another 3% on December 1.

Billing runs a year behind, so what came due in 2026 belongs to tax year 2025. Manufactured homes run on a different schedule, with taxes for the current year due in early March and late August.

  • Online: e-check carries no fee. Debit cards cost a flat $2.95 and credit cards 2.3% with a $1.50 minimum.
  • Phone: 1-877-738-1212. Enter an asterisk for each space in the parcel number.
  • Mail: Cuyahoga County Treasurer, PO Box 94547, Cleveland, OH 44101. The Treasurer warns that a postmark shows when the sorting machine handled the envelope, so send early or have a clerk hand-stamp it.
  • In person or drop box: 2079 East 9th Street. Satellite payment locations open only during the January-February and July-August collection seasons.

How does a Cleveland owner challenge a valuation?

The Board of Revision takes valuation complaints from January 1 to March 31, moving to the next business day if March 31 is a weekend. Its preferred method is the e-file portal, which needs only an email address and phone number and skips the notary step. Paper complaints go to 2079 East 9th Street, 2nd Floor, or by fax to 216-443-8282, and office hours are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

The board encourages the state's DTE 1 form. Question 9 wants your opinion of value as one exact number; a blank or a range gets the complaint dismissed. The burden of proof rests with the owner, so bring a recent sale price, a listing agreement from the past three years, an appraisal, or repair estimates. Mailed complaints need a United States Postal Service postmark of March 31 or earlier; a private meter mark from a courier is rejected.

The board cannot change a rate, a levy or a penalty.

What does a seller need from the City of Cleveland before closing?

Section 367.12 of the city's code, as cited on the application, requires anyone selling or transferring real property to hand the buyer a Certificate of Disclosure. The city's application lists a $60 fee for each structure on the lot, with the escrow or transferring agent filing it on the city's online portal.

Part F of the form, filled in by city staff, covers the lot's legal use, the number of structures, a Certificate of Occupancy where it applies, any historic district status, any condemnation or open violation, and lead hazard control orders. When violations are open, the buyer signs the notice and attaches it to the purchase agreement. The form also asks whether the house is a rental with a current registration and, for rentals built before 1978, a lead safe certificate.

  • Anyone who buys to rent must register the address with Building and Housing once the deed transfers.
  • A house left empty goes on the Vacant Property Registry within 15 days after the transfer.
  • The city's rental registration page lists $70 per unit, renewed yearly, with renewals opening after January 1 and payment due by March 31.

An owner who lives beyond Cuyahoga and the neighboring counties must name a Local Agent in Charge, and a building with four or more rental units also needs a heating system inspection certificate.

What do the Census figures say about Cleveland?

The Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate is 363,608 residents, below the 372,635 counted at the April 2020 base. Renters outnumber owners.

Cleveland city in Census QuickFacts (population for July 1, 2025; other rows 2020-2024)
MeasureCleveland
Population estimate363,608
Change since the April 2020 base-2.4%
Homeownership rate41.7%
Median value of owner-occupied homes$102,000
Median gross rent$945
Median household income$40,801
Persons in poverty30.6%

The city counts 169,683 households of about 2.09 people each. Because fewer than half of homes are lived in by owners, the registration and disclosure rules above touch a large share of sales.

What if a Cleveland owner is behind on property tax?

Current tax unpaid ten calendar days past the close of collection draws a 10% penalty. Older delinquent tax runs at 12% a year under the Treasurer's written order, and continued nonpayment can end in tax foreclosure and a sheriff's sale.

The first tool is a payment plan. Bring photo ID and a voided check or bank statement for automatic monthly deductions, and certified funds if the parcel is in foreclosure or a tax lien. The current year's tax must be paid on time as well, and while a plan is active the parcel is not offered at a tax certificate sale or by the sheriff. The Treasurer holds Last Chance Payment Plan classes for owners seeking a third contract. Residents 67 and older earning under $70,000 may qualify for a separate Taxpayer Assistance Program.

Cleveland's residential tax abatement program, run under Ordinance 482-2022 since January 1, 2024, offers 85% to 100% of the increased assessed taxes on permitted improvements, with single-family abatement possibly capped at home values between $350,000 and $450,000. A seller who rehabilitated a house with a city permit should ask the county whether an abatement attaches to the parcel, and for how long it runs.

What does Cuyahoga County charge to record a Cleveland deed?

Transfer and Recording, at 216-443-2060, takes new recordings until 4:00 p.m., half an hour before the rest of the office closes. Every transfer needs a DTE 100 Statement of Value and Receipt, or a DTE 100-EX when an exemption from the conveyance fee applies. The recording fee rose on October 24, 2024 under Ohio Senate Bill 94 to $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after that. County staff cannot give legal advice, and the Ohio Supreme Court treats drafting a deed as the practice of law.

The Fiscal Officer also offers Property Alerts, which notify an owner about potentially fraudulent filings against real property, and a Great Estates Program with guidance on avoiding unnecessary cost and delay in settling an estate. Owners who inherited a Cleveland house may find that second program useful before listing.

More questions about Cleveland, OH Property Tax Guide

Which office do I pay for a Cleveland property tax bill?

Pay the Cuyahoga County Treasurer, not the City of Cleveland. Payment options are online, by phone at 1-877-738-1212, by mail to PO Box 94547, in person at 2079 East 9th Street, or through the drop box there.

When is the Cleveland valuation complaint deadline?

March 31, or the next business day if it falls on a weekend. The window opens January 1 and the Board of Revision prefers e-filing on form DTE 1.

What is the Cleveland Certificate of Disclosure?

It is a city document required when a house is sold or transferred, with a listed fee of $60 per structure. It tells the buyer about open violations, condemnation history, rental registration and lead-safe status.

What does Cleveland charge to register a rental?

The city's rental registration page lists $70 per unit for non-owner-occupied residential property. It is renewed yearly, and fees are due by March 31.

What interest does Cuyahoga County charge on delinquent tax?

Per the Filing Instructions page: 2026 BOR filing season opens Aug 25, 2026 and closes Mar 31, 2027; submit by e-filing, email (BOR@franklincountyohio.gov), mail (373 S. High St., 20th Fl., Columbus) or fax (614-525-6252).. See the official page.

Columbus by the numbers

Who sends a Columbus homeowner a property tax bill?

The Franklin County Treasurer sends it, and the Franklin County Auditor decides the value behind it. Columbus does not bill property tax itself. Franklin County holds the bulk of Columbus, yet Wikipedia lists Delaware and Fairfield counties among the places Columbus covers, so a house near the city's northern or southern edge may be taxed through a different county's auditor and treasurer. Check the county printed on your last bill before you call anyone.

OfficeJobContact it publishes
Franklin County AuditorSets values, takes tax reduction applications, runs the Board of RevisionBoard of Revision: 614-525-3913, 373 S. High St., 20th Floor
Franklin County TreasurerMails bills, collects payments, handles penalties614-525-3438, 373 S. High St., 17th Floor, hours of 8:00 to 5:00 on weekdays

The Treasurer's tax bill page explains the yearly sequence. Voters decide levies in November, the Board of Elections certifies the results, the Auditor and the Ohio Department of Taxation settle rates in early December, and the Treasurer mails bills later that month. In Franklin County, 440,173 parcels are on the tax list, and 239,956 of them are paid through a mortgage company, so many owners never see a paper bill.

When are Columbus property taxes due?

Tax year 2025 was collected in 2026, and the Treasurer's collection dates page lists February 28 and July 20. The Treasurer's real estate tax page gives March 2, 2026 for the first half instead. The Treasurer's due date FAQ says the due dates changed in 2026 while the amount owed did not, so confirm the exact date for your own parcel on your bill.

Owners can pay once a year, in two halves or monthly. The Treasurer says 171,000 parcels sit in its monthly budget pay program. If a mortgage lender escrows your taxes, the FAQ reminds owners to confirm that the lender's escrow account matches the new dates, because that responsibility stays with the taxpayer.

Payment is flexible. The due date FAQ says owners can pay by mail, in person at the Treasurer's office or electronically, and that an existing payment plan or delinquent tax contract continues as agreed when dates change. Prepayments are applied to the account as usual, and owners can pay any time after the bills are published and before the due date.

Late payments bring penalties under ORC 323.121. The statute sets a ten percent penalty on the unpaid balance of a late half, and it halves that penalty if the full amount arrives within ten days. The Treasurer warns that never getting a bill is no defense against the penalty, and anyone still waiting for one is asked to phone 614-525-3438. Checking the mailing address the Treasurer holds for the parcel is worth doing after any move.

How does a Columbus owner challenge the value?

By filing a Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property, form DTE 1, with the Franklin County Board of Revision. The Auditor's filing page says the 2026 filing season opens August 25, 2026 and closes March 31, 2027. Its tax reduction page adds that the board takes complaints from mid-November through March 31 every year. Residential owners also attach a Residential Data Sheet.

Ohio revalues property every six years, with an update at the three-year midpoint, according to the Treasurer's real estate tax page. Between those updates a value changes only if the property is altered, demolished or changed by a Board of Revision decision. The Board of Revision weighs the evidence an owner submits.

The Auditor's FAQ describes what happens after a win:

  • There is a 30-day appeal window after the board's decision, and refund processing starts when it ends
  • Refunds are usually processed within three more weeks, not counting mail time
  • Ohio law sends the refund to whoever actually paid the tax, which can be a mortgage company or title company
  • If the property transferred, taxes still owed on it are credited before any refund is issued
  • A payment made after the due date goes to the Treasurer's surplus account, and the owner must ask the Treasurer to release it

Which Franklin County tax reductions can a Columbus owner use?

The Auditor's tax reduction page lists a set of programs, each with its own state form. The ones that apply to a Columbus house are:

  • The homestead exemption for senior citizens, disabled persons and surviving spouses, form DTE 105A
  • A homestead exemption for veterans with a total disability rating, form DTE 105I
  • The owner-occupancy reduction, form DTE 105C, for a house the owner lives in as a primary home when the tax year begins
  • A damaged property value reduction, form DTE 26, for storm or fire damage
  • Current agricultural use value for working farmland, form DTE 109, which seldom fits a city lot

Anyone selling should find out whether the property carries one of these reductions. The buyer's value statement under ORC 319.202 asks the seller whether the house receives one.

Who handles the tax bill at a Columbus closing?

The Franklin County Auditor says plainly that it is not involved in real estate closings and does not prorate tax payments. The title company or closing agent splits the year between buyer and seller and pays any amount that is due. Ask the Franklin County Treasurer for a current payoff before closing, and look at the parcel for any delinquency or tax contract so the title company knows what to clear.

At the transfer itself, the grantor pays the auditor's conveyance fee under ORC 319.54, which is the larger of $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, with any county transfer tax added on top. The auditor then moves the parcel into the buyer's name on the tax list. The Auditor's FAQ also notes that a recent transfer can complicate refunds, so tell the title company about any open Board of Revision case.

What is Columbus like for a seller?

Columbus was settled on February 14, 1812, and incorporated on February 10, 1816. It sits where the Scioto and Olentangy rivers meet, on flat glaciated ground, and Wikipedia notes a long history of flooding that includes the Great Flood of 1913. The city has the largest land area of any Ohio city, a result of annexing suburbs that needed city water, and the city now spans three counties.

QuickFacts shows a July 2025 estimate of 938,396 residents, 3.6% above the 2020 base, along with these housing figures:

  • Owned homes carry a typical value of $252,900 across 2020 to 2024
  • Owner-occupied rate: 44.1%, so most households rent
  • Median gross rent: $1,295 a month
  • 390,528 households earning a median of $66,082
  • Bachelor's degree or higher among adults 25 and over: 38.2%

Every figure is a citywide number, and single neighborhoods run on both sides of it. Ask for a written offer or a local appraisal when you need a price for one address, and bring the latest tax bill to that conversation.

More questions about Columbus, OH Property Tax Guide

Which county bills property tax for my Columbus house?

Usually Franklin County, but parts of Columbus lie in Delaware and Fairfield counties. Read your last bill to see which county treasurer issued it.

What were the 2026 due dates for Franklin County real estate tax?

The collection dates page shows February 28 and July 20 for tax year 2025, while the real estate tax page shows March 2 and July 20. Confirm the first-half date on your own bill.

Can I appeal my Columbus property value?

Yes. You file form DTE 1 with the Franklin County Board of Revision, and the 2026 season closes March 31, 2027. The Board of Revision phone number is 614-525-3913.

Does the county prorate taxes when I sell?

No. The Franklin County Auditor says it does not prorate taxes or take part in closings. The title company or closing agent splits the bill between buyer and seller.

What if I never received a tax bill?

The tax is still owed, and a penalty can still apply, because Ohio law treats a bill that never arrived as no excuse. Call the Treasurer at 614-525-3438 to get the amount.

Owe Dayton Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who bills what in Dayton

  • Montgomery County Auditor handles assessment.

Due dates

First half collection due Feb 13, 2026; second half due July 24, 2026 (billed one year in arrears).. See the official page.

Challenging your assessment

Complaints can be filed between January 1 and March 31 (BOR Process page); complaint form via Auditor's Office.. See the official page.

Local notes

Behind on Dayton property tax?

Get My Cash Offer →

Dayton by the numbers

Who bills and who values property tax for a Dayton house?

Property tax in Dayton is a county matter, and Dayton happens to be where the county seat sits. One Montgomery County office sets the value of your house, and a second sends the bill and takes the payment. Billing questions reach Taxpayer Services at 937-225-4010, option 1, while value questions reach the auditor at 937-225-4326.

The treasurer's own annual report counts more than 250,000 real estate parcels under its collection, a volume that explains the phone, online and drop box options.

QuestionWhere to goPhone
Reading or paying a billMontgomery County Treasurer, Taxpayer Services937-225-4010, option 1
Behind on taxes, payment plansTreasurer, delinquency specialist937-225-4010, option 2
Value, levies, tax increase questionsMontgomery County Auditor937-225-4326
Valuation complaint formAuditor's Board of Revision937-496-6856
Solid waste charge on the billSemi-Annual Property Charge line937-224-8463

Source: the Montgomery County treasurer's question pages.

When are Dayton property taxes due?

Two payments a year come due in February and July, with the bills mailed in January and June. The 2026 deadlines were February 13 and July 24, and both are behind us. The treasurer publishes a collection timeline for later years.

Montgomery County bills a full year in arrears. A first-half bill pays for January through June of the prior calendar year, and a second-half bill pays for July through December of that same prior year. Ask the treasurer which periods a pending sale touches before you set the closing date.

  • Paying the whole year in February earns no discount.
  • Any half left unpaid after its due date draws a 10 percent penalty.
  • Halves can differ in size, because some assessments are collected on the first-half bill alone.

What payment help does the Montgomery County Treasurer offer?

A prepayment plan lets owners without past-due taxes pay in monthly installments, by mailed payment or by automatic withdrawal. Enrollment closes 60 days before a due date and requires current taxes to be paid. Coupons are mailed in early March and early August.

Owners who are behind can sign a delinquent payment contract that covers new taxes as they fall due while the older balance is paid down, without added interest and penalty. A sold lien is a different matter. The treasurer cannot accept payments on it, so you work with the lien holder, and the parcel record keeps showing the lien as sold until it is formally released, even after the holder is paid.

The treasurer's payment options page names online payment, a drop box, in-person and mail payment, phone payment, the monthly prepayment program and past-due plans.

How do you appeal a Dayton property value?

The Board of Revision, which sits within the auditor's office, supplies the complaint application; the treasurer's page gives 937-496-6856 for requesting one by mail. ORC 5715.19 puts the deadline at March 31 of the following tax year or the end of first-half collection, whichever is later, and the treasurer's page describes a window from January 2 to March 31.

Complaints are investigated and may go to a formal hearing where the owner must justify the claim. Values can move up as well as down. The statute lets you pay on your claimed value while the case is open and gives the board 180 days after the deadline to rule on an original complaint.

A lower value can still come with a higher bill, the treasurer notes, since levies passed in your school or local district raise the effective rate.

How do you change a mailing address or get payment records in Dayton?

Ohio law wants a mailing-address change for tax bills in writing, and the treasurer provides a Change of Address form. A seller can file it once a closing date is set so the next bill is not mailed to a house that has changed hands.

When a lender pays your taxes from escrow, the withheld amount shows on the lender's 1099. If you pay directly and need records, ask the treasurer's Taxpayer Services line for an itemization, because none is mailed automatically. A bill that reaches you while a lender is responsible should go to the lender's attention, and the lender will request its own copy.

Real estate tax is shared among counties, cities, villages, school districts and special districts, and the treasurer's page says it funds schools, police and fire protection, roads, libraries and parks.

Is there a senior or disability tax reduction in Dayton?

Yes. Montgomery County's Homestead Reduction Program serves owners aged 65 or older and owners who are totally and permanently disabled, and only a primary residence the owner occupies qualifies. The treasurer's page refers readers to the county homestead page for the application, so check there or call the auditor first.

The reduction also shows up at closing. Through ORC 319.202, the conveyance paperwork asks whether the seller's tax carries it, and a yes brings a sworn statement from both sides. A buyer who cannot claim it faces a higher bill than the seller paid.

What is Dayton like for a seller, and how does that affect value?

Dayton was founded in 1796 on the Great Miami River. Its 2020 census profile shows:

  • 137,644 residents, the sixth-largest city in Ohio.
  • 57,751 households and 68,899 housing units, of which 16.2 percent were vacant.
  • A median age of 34.9 years, with 41.1 percent of households made up of one person.

The city's ten historic neighborhoods include the Oregon District, Wright Dunbar, Dayton View, Grafton Hill, McPherson Town, Webster Station, Huffman, Kenilworth, St. Anne's Hill and South Park, and they hold many single-family houses in styles from Craftsman to Colonial Revival. Dayton Public Schools runs 34 schools, and the Dayton International Airport, Wright-Patterson Air Force Base and the healthcare systems anchor local employment.

Two weather facts shape upkeep. The 1913 flood led to the Miami Conservancy District's dams and pumps, and the Memorial Day 2019 tornado outbreak produced an EF4 that crossed Dayton and nearby communities. Keep records of roof, drainage and basement repairs so a buyer can see what was done.

Climate adds wear. The airport station records about 41 inches of precipitation a year, peaking in May, plus a normal 23 inches of snow, mostly November through March. Summers are hot and humid, and the area sees tornadoes from spring to fall along with floods and severe thunderstorms. Downtown's wide, straight streets date to the days of ox-drawn wagons, and the University of Dayton, Wright State University and Sinclair Community College are among the area's major schools, along with the Air Force Institute of Technology at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.

More questions about Dayton, OH Property Tax Guide

Does the City of Dayton collect property tax?

No. The Montgomery County Treasurer bills and collects the tax and the Montgomery County Auditor sets the value. Contact the treasurer's Taxpayer Services line at 937-225-4010, option 1, about a bill.

What happens if I miss a Dayton property tax due date?

A 10 percent penalty applies to any first-half or second-half payment not paid in full by its due date. Call the treasurer's delinquency line at 937-225-4010, option 2, to ask about a payment plan.

Why is my Dayton tax bill a year behind?

Montgomery County bills one full year in arrears. The first-half bill covers January through June of the previous year and the second-half bill covers July through December of that year.

Can I sell a Dayton house if a tax lien was sold?

Yes, but the treasurer cannot take payments on a sold lien. Contact the lien holder for payoff terms and confirm the lien shows as released on the parcel record after payment.

How do I dispute my Dayton property value?

File a complaint with the Montgomery County Auditor's Board of Revision, which you can request by calling 937-496-6856. The filing deadline is March 31 of the following tax year or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later.

Challenging your assessment

Board of Revision filing period is Jan 1 - Mar 31 (2026 shown); file DTE 1/1M/2 online via SmartFile, or paper/notarized by mail or email to auditorbor@co.lucas.oh.us.. See the official page.

Local notes

Behind on Toledo property tax?

Get My Cash Offer →

Toledo by the numbers

Who sends the property tax bill for a house inside Toledo?

Lucas County sends it, and the city does not. The County Auditor sets the value and the County Treasurer mails the bill, and both offices are in One Government Center downtown, the Auditor in Suite 600 and the Treasurer in Suite 500. The Auditor's line is 419-213-4406 and the Treasurer's is 419-213-4305, as the Auditor's tax page lists them.

Toledo's own Division of Taxation, in Suite 2070 of the same building, handles a different levy: the city income tax. Check the letterhead on anything that arrives. This page covers the county bill that attaches to a Toledo address. The Auditor's property tax page adds that the Auditor sends collected money out to every subdivision in the county after the Treasurer collects it.

What kind of city is Toledo for someone selling a house?

Toledo straddles the Maumee River where it enters Maumee Bay, the westernmost inlet of Lake Erie. According to Wikipedia, settlers founded the city in 1833, and it was re-founded in 1837 after the Toledo War put it in Ohio. The Miami and Erie Canal arrived in 1845, glass makers followed in the 1880s, and the port ranks fifth busiest on the Great Lakes. The ground sits north of the old Great Black Swamp, in the sandy Oak Openings region.

Wikipedia lists dozens of Toledo neighborhoods, among them Old West End, a National Register historic district of Victorian and Arts and Crafts houses, plus Point Place, Ottawa, Uptown, Five Points, Old Orchard, Westgate, Reynolds Corners, East Toledo, the Warehouse District, Secor Gardens near the University of Toledo and many more. Sylvania, Maumee, Oregon, Perrysburg and Ottawa Hills sit just outside the city line.

The Toledo City School District covers most of the city across 70 square miles and enrolled more than 23,000 students in 2019, making it the fourth largest in Ohio. Washington Local serves the north end. Jeep's Toledo Complex, health care and the university anchor the job base, and glass names such as Owens Corning keep the old identity alive.

How do the Census numbers for Toledo read?

Toledo city figures from Census QuickFacts, with 2025 estimates and 2020 to 2024 survey data
MeasureToledo
Population, July 2025 estimate263,423
Change since April 2020 basedown 2.8 percent
Owner-occupied housing rate53.3 percent
Median value, owner-occupied homes$114,500
Median gross rent$901
Median household income$49,724
Persons in poverty24.3 percent
People per square mile, 20203,365.4

With owners in only 53.3 percent of homes, rentals shape many Toledo blocks. Treat every figure above as a citywide midpoint, since a house near Old West End and one near the river can sit far from it.

Snowfall runs near 37 inches a year, January averages 27.5 degrees and July 75.4, and the lake usually freezes over. A buyer's inspector will likely look hard at the roof, gutters and furnace of an older Toledo house.

When are Toledo-area property taxes due, and how are they paid?

The bill splits into two installments. The Treasurer listed January 31 and July 31, 2026 for the 2025 taxes, since Ohio bills a year in arrears. A mailed payment needs a postmark on or before the date, and web or phone payments made after 8:00 p.m. Eastern wait for the next business day. Money takes 5 to 7 days to show against your parcel.

The Treasurer's payment page lists these channels:

  • Online by debit card, credit card or eCheck. Cards carry a 2.5 percent fee and an eCheck costs 50 cents.
  • By phone at 1-866-288-9803, with fees.
  • In person on the fifth floor of One Government Center. Cash, checks and money orders carry no fee.
  • By mail in the envelope that came with the bill, parcel number on the check.
  • At the silver drop box at 640 Jackson Street, across from Government Center.
  • At Genoa Bank or WesBanco, in January and July only, with the exact amount and the original bill.

The Treasurer cautions that postmarks now usually reflect the first machine pass, which may fall a day or more after you mail the envelope. Send it early, request a hand stamp at the post office window, or pick another channel.

What does the Inflation Cap Credit on a Toledo bill mean?

It is a state-law reduction under R.C. 319.303 that appears as its own line labeled with those words. The Treasurer's HB186 page says no application is needed, not every property gets it, and it is separate from both the homestead exemption and the owner-occupancy credit. The credit amount varies with property value, taxing district, school district and the taxes that qualify, and the Treasurer cannot adjust it.

Special assessments also ride on the bill after rollbacks. The Auditor says they cover snow and leaf removal, alleyway cleaning and sidewalk repair, among others, and they count as fees rather than taxes, so even tax-exempt parcels may owe them. Rates themselves come from levies voters passed. The Auditor describes the basic math as 35 percent of market value multiplied by the district rate, followed by the rollbacks and credits. The Auditor also notes that the owner-occupied credit and the homestead exemption apply after the House Bill 920 rollbacks.

Does the Toledo income tax matter when I sell?

It matters only if you are a Toledo filer. The city's rate has been 2.5 percent since January 1, 2021 under Toledo Municipal Code 1905.011, and the 2025 individual deadline was April 15, 2026, per the city tax page. It is a separate bill from the county's real estate tax. Appointments with the Finance Department go through Engage Toledo at 419-936-2020. Engage Toledo is also the city's request channel for tall grass, blight and structure concerns, which is worth knowing before a showing if a lot has drawn complaints.

Which Lucas County steps come before a Toledo closing?

Three county tasks come up for most sellers:

  • Rental registration. Under R.C. 5323, any livable structure that is not your primary home must be registered as a rental or carry a filed exception, with fines possible otherwise. Look up an address in the Auditor's AREIS database.
  • Deed transfer. Staff at the Auditor's office are barred from drafting a deed. The Engineer's Tax Map Department on the seventh floor approves the legal description, the Recorder checks the fee amounts, and the Auditor on the sixth floor takes the conveyance form. Both buyer and seller attend with unexpired photo ID.
  • Fees. The Auditor's page puts the conveyance fee at $4.00 per $1,000 of price with a $0.50 charge per parcel, and gives the deed recording fee as $39.00 for two pages and $8.00 for every page after.

Mobile home titles need all current-year taxes paid before transfer.

What if the tax on a Toledo house is behind?

The Treasurer's Delinquent Installment Payment Plan lets an owner-occupant pay past-due tax over up to 24 months with 20 percent down, and plans are not issued in the ten days right after a due date. An exception request is answered in most cases within ten business days.

The county can also sell delinquent liens as tax certificates. The Treasurer's FAQ says a notice does not mean the house was sold and that the office generally keeps owner-occupied homes and homestead properties out of such sales. The Treasurer must give the record owner at least 30 days' written notice before a negotiated sale. The tax lien hotline is 419-574-6022. Separately, the Lucas County Land Bank, founded in 2010, works to return vacant and tax-delinquent properties to use.

More questions about Toledo, OH Property Tax Guide

Does the City of Toledo bill my property tax?

No. Lucas County's Auditor values the house and the Treasurer bills it. The city collects income tax through its Division of Taxation.

How soon does a mailed Lucas County tax payment post?

Allow 5 to 7 days. Timeliness turns on the postmark, and the Postal Service may stamp the envelope a day or more after you drop it off, so mail well ahead of the due date.

Is the Inflation Cap Credit the same as homestead?

No. It is automatic under R.C. 319.303 and separate from the homestead exemption and owner-occupancy credit. Your bill shows it on its own line when it applies.

Must a Toledo rental be registered before I sell it?

Yes. Rentals belong in the Lucas County Auditor's registry, and a property that is not your primary home but is not a rental needs an exception on file. Skipping it may bring fines.

What is the Toledo city income tax rate?

2.5 percent since January 1, 2021. It is separate from the county real estate bill.
